name: Slow bulking / slow growth to avoid stretch marks

card.summary: Gaining weight or muscle gradually in the belief that it lowers the chance of stretch marks; rapid growth is a recognised risk factor, but no trial has tested slow bulking.
card.note: Genetics and hormones also influence striae; no trials of gain rate on stretch marks were found.

quick.overview:
Some lifters and growing teenagers aim to gain size slowly to reduce the chance of stretch marks (striae). The idea rests on the understanding that striae are scars caused by the skin stretching quickly.[1]

Wikipedia lists weight gain (fat or muscle), adolescent growth spurts, pregnancy and bodybuilding among risk factors, alongside genetics and hormones. No study was found that tests whether a slower rate of gain changes the incidence.
quick.mechanism: Stretch marks appear to be caused by stretching of the skin, with tearing of the dermis; elevated cortisol, which can reduce collagen and elastin production, is also implicated.[1] Slow gain is proposed to give skin more time to adapt.
quick.risks: Slow bulking itself carries no particular documented harm. Wikipedia reports that a Cochrane review found no evidence that creams or oils prevent stretch marks in pregnancy, and no clearly useful treatment exists once they form.[1]

lead: Slow bulking, or slow growth, refers to gaining weight or muscle gradually with the aim of avoiding stretch marks (striae). Stretch marks are dermal scars thought to be caused by rapid stretching of the skin.[1]

Wikipedia lists rapid weight gain, adolescent growth spurts, pregnancy, bodybuilding and hormone therapy among recognised risk factors, with genetics and conditions that raise cortisol also contributing.[1] No published trial was found comparing different rates of weight or muscle gain with stretch mark incidence.

paras: Stretch marks are scars from tearing of the dermis during rapid growth. Higher levels of cortisone reduce skin pliability and can stop fibroblasts from making the collagen and elastin that keep skin taut.[1] Corticosteroid use and conditions such as Cushing's syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Marfan syndrome may raise the likelihood.[1]

Risk factors listed include weight gain from fat or muscle, adolescent growth spurts, pregnancy, bodybuilding and hormone replacement therapy. In pregnancy, a 2006 study of 324 women linked striae with young maternal age, high BMI, gestational weight gain over 15 kg and higher birth weight, and genetics including family history appear predictive.[1]

Proponents of gradual gain reason that a smaller rate of change gives the skin time to adapt. This reasoning is consistent with the stretching mechanism but has not been tested directly in trials of gain rate. Nutrition (zinc, protein and vitamins A, C and D) is suggested on Wikipedia as potentially helpful, though it is described as a suggestion rather than established prevention.[1]

A Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia found no evidence that creams or oils prevent stretch marks in pregnancy, and a 2014 review found no clearly useful treatment for established marks. Topical tretinoin has been effective in several studies on early marks, but is a teratogen and is not used in pregnancy.[1]
No studies found examining slow versus rapid bulking and stretch mark incidence. Related research on pregnancy and adolescent growth is summarised above.[1]
